3. The only point involved for decision is whether the suit which was dismissed for default for non-appearance of the plaintiff can be restored under section 151 CPC instead of filing a Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 9 CPC. 

 5. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that it is very much clear from the order dated 2-3-1996 that the suit was taken up for peremptory hearing and plaintiff was absent and the defendant was present. After the order of dismissal of the suit, the plaintiff should have come with a Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is legal and apt forum for the relief. Therefore, the impugned order passed under section151 CPC restoring the suit is illegal and it has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 6. In support' of his submission Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Counsel, cites the decisions in the case of Bangladesh Shilpa Bank vs. Bangladesh Hotels Ltd., reported in 38 DLR (AD) 70, Azizur Rahman vs. Janata Bank, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 252, Rezaul Huq Molla vs. Afizullah Mollah and others, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 74, Punjab Ali Pramanik and others vs. Mohd. Mokarrum Hossain, 29. DLR (SC) 185 On the basis of those decisions Mr. Ahmed submits that the Appellate Division and the High Court Division have consistently held that when there is specific legal remedy as provided by the Code under Order 9 rule 9 for restoration of the suit after dismissal for default, the orders of the trial Court granted under section151 CPC is prima facie illegal. He has also drawn my attention to all the aforesaid decisions wherein it has been held, according to him, that even for the ends of justice relief cannot be granted under section 151 CPC restoring a suit dismissed for default 

 7. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel for the opposite party submits that even conceding the spirit of the aforesaid decisions he wants to make a distinction in the instant case with those cases as cited by the learned Counsel for the petitioner in view of the fact that in the operative portion of the impugned order passed it has been written by the trial Court as follows: 

 8. So, Mr. Mahbuey Alam, the learned Counsel, submitted that although the provision of section 151 CPC cannot be invoked and jurisdiction under it cannot be ordinately exercised to give relief but in the present circumstances when mistake has been committed by the court itself, the trial Court can exercise his discretion under section 151 CPC and can give relief by way of restoring the suit to its file and number. In this particular case, the trial Court has dismissed the suit finding that the plaintiff was not willing to proceed with the suit, but it is beyond record and he also submits that within four corners of the two applications which were filed on the date of peremptory hearing for adjournment of the date of the suit (which are Annexures 'A' and 'AI' to this application) so this is an error apparent on the face of the record, committed by the trial Court itself. Therefore, according to Mr. Alam, the trial Court has legally exercised his discretion under section 151 CPC. Mr. Alam, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, also focuses his arguments very forcefully saying that after the last amendment of section 115 of CPC only when there is failure of justice, the High Court Division should interfere under section 115 CPC. In the instant litigation by the impugned order, the trial Court has restored the suit giving opportunity to both parties who are full brothers to fight on merits. So there is nothing in the order resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 9. In support of his submission Mr. Alam cites the decisions in the cases of Syed Azizul Hoque alias Nanna Meah vs. Sonali Bank, reported in 1990 BLD 247, Aynuddin and others vs. Azizuddin and others, reported in 43 DLR 207, Kazi Motiur Rahman and others vs. Din Islam, reported in 43 DLR 128 and in the case Trading Corporation of Bangladesh vs. Syed Sajeduzzaman, reported in 40 DLR 406 and lastly, he has cited the decision in the case of Md. Bonde Ali Khan vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 1986 BLD 232. Their Lordships in the decisions cited by Mr. Alam have dealt with two aspects in the particular litigation. One being whether the dismissal order is for absence of the plaintiff simpliciter, secondly, whether it has been caused due to mistake of the court itself and on that platform their Lordships have considered the scope to exercise jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Their Lordships are of the opinion that when there is mistake of the court itself, the trial Court can exercise its discretion under section 151 CPC. In this case, I am of the view that the trial Court himself committed mistake in dismissing the suit finding that the plaintiff was not willing to proceed with the same and, as such, the trial Court legally has exercised his jurisdiction under section 151 CPC. Secondly, I find that by restoration of the suit no failure of justice has been caused. In my view, it is not unjust, when two parties come before the court for justice, the final and effective order in the litigation if passed after hearing of both the parties on merits. 

 12. My opinion, in fine, is that in the present case, mistake has been committed by the court and rightly and legally it has been cured by restoring the suit itself and in that view of the matter, there is no failure of justice in the impugned order. So I am not inclined to interfere. Therefore, the argument of Mr. Sultan Ahmed having no force is repelled and that of Mr. Mahbubey Alam is accepted.
